extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy; readers of Kant
extracted.subtask_description: Expository introduction to Kant's Critique of Judgement, laying out the faculties (Understanding, Judgement, Reason), the division of philosophy (theoretical vs practical), and the a priori principles (notably purposiveness) that govern reflective and aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of philosophy into theoretical and practical
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy is correctly divided into theoretical (Natural Philosophy) and practical (Moral Philosophy) parts because they rest on specifically distinct concepts: natural concepts for theoretical cognition and the concept of freedom for practical legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The division depends on whether the concepts that furnish the object of rational cognition are natural concepts (giving theoretical principles a priori) or the concept of freedom (giving morally practical laws). Examples of technically practical activities (housekeeping, farming, statesmanship, arts of experiment) are NOT parts of practical philosophy if their principles are derived from natural concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between technically practical and morally practical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Technically practical rules (rules of art, skill, prudence) rest on natural concepts and are corollaries of theoretical philosophy; morally practical precepts rest on the concept of freedom and are laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technically practical precepts concern what is possible according to natural concepts and are contingent/empirical (e.g., prescribing diet, statesmanship). Morally practical laws are based on the supersensible concept of freedom and are not empirical; they constitute the proper content of practical Philosophy (doctrine of Morals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement defined as the faculty subsuming particular under universal
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgement is the faculty of thinking the particular as contained under the universal. If the universal is given, the judgement that subsumes the particular under it is determinant; if only the particular is given and the universal must be found, the judgement is reflective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition sets up two distinct operations of judgement (determinant and reflective) and grounds subsequent discussion of how judgement supplies principles a priori.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinant vs reflective judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinant Judgement subsumes particulars under given universal transcendental laws (no need to find a law). Reflective Judgement ascends from particular empirical cases to find a universal (it must supply a principle from itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinant judgement operates under laws prescribed by the Understanding; reflective judgement requires a principle that cannot be borrowed from experience and must be given by Judgement itself (a subjective a priori principle) to establish unity of empirical principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic (aesthetical) judgement concerns feeling of pleasure and pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic judgements (taste) concern the Beautiful and the Sublime in Nature or Art and link the cognitive faculty to the feeling of pleasure and pain; they are central to a Critique of Judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The investigation is transcendental (not aimed at cultivation of taste) and asks whether Judgement supplies principles a priori for such feelings. Aesthetic judgements do not contribute to knowledge of things but belong to the cognitive faculty and point to an immediate reference to pleasure/pain without conflating with practical desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Judgement must be self-derived (not from concepts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A principle peculiar to Judgement must not be derived a priori from concepts (these belong to the Understanding); Judgement must furnish a concept of its own that serves as a rule for application, though not an objective rule prescribing to things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Judgement concerns application of concepts rather than their formation, its principle must produce a rule 'from itself'—a reflective, subjective a priori principle—rather than borrow from other faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness of nature as the transcendental principle of Judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of Judgement (in respect of the form of things under empirical laws) is the purposiveness of nature in its manifoldness: we must represent nature as if an Understanding supplied the ground of unity of its empirical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This purposiveness is a particular a priori concept originating in reflective Judgement; it is not an attribution of actual purposive intent to natural objects but a regulative idea guiding reflection to think empirical manifold as potentially systematizable under laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness is a subjective a priori principle, giving law to Judgement not to nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of purposiveness does not ascribe properties to objects; it represents how we must proceed in reflection upon objects of nature to achieve a connected experience. It is therefore a subjective principle (a maxim) of Judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgement uses purposiveness to think the unity of contingent empirical laws; it prescribes a way of judging (how we ought to judge) rather than prescribing anything objective to nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxims of the Judgement (heuristic rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common maxims underlying Judgement include: 'Nature takes the shortest way' (lex parsimoniae); 'Nature makes no leaps' (lex continui in natura); 'Principles beyond necessity are not to be multiplied' (principia praeter necessitatem non sunt multiplicanda).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are expressions of the transcendental concept of purposiveness and serve as heuristic maxims indicating the necessary manner in which we must reflect to secure unity of empirical laws when a priori demonstration is unavailable. They are not derived psychologically from how we judge but prescribe how we ought to judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendental vs metaphysical principle distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A transcendental principle represents a priori the universal condition under which things can be Objects of our cognition; a metaphysical principle is an a priori condition under which empirically-given objects can be further determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the principle that changes must have a cause is transcendental (grounds possibility of experience); the claim that changes must have an external cause is metaphysical (requires empirical concept of body). This distinction helps classify the principle of purposiveness as transcendental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective Judgement assumes unity of empirical laws for system of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflective Judgement must presuppose for its special use that what appears contingent in particular empirical laws nonetheless contains a unity of law such that the manifold can form a possible system of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because universal laws of nature (Categories) do not fully determine specific empirical laws, reflective Judgement posits a principle of unity (purposiveness) to enable systematic subordination of empirical laws into a coherent experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a Transcendental Deduction of the principle of purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of the purposiveness of nature, being a transcendental principle of Judgement, requires a Transcendental Deduction to ground why such judging is valid in the sources of cognition a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One cannot account for the necessity of these maxims by a psychological account of how we judge; their objective logical necessity (how we ought to judge) demands a transcendental justification rooted in the faculties of cognition.
